items.title: entry: Apply Hardy-Weinberg, testcross, mapping, and biometry
items.prompt: A problem gives the frequency of a recessive phenotype in a large model population and asks for the expected heterozygote frequency. Which method is most direct?
options: Hardy–Weinberg equations
A testcross with a homozygous recessive tester
A crossover-frequency linkage calculation
A backcross between F1 offspring and one parent
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: guided: Apply Hardy-Weinberg, testcross, mapping, and biometry
items.prompt: Under Hardy–Weinberg, a recessive phenotype has frequency 0.16. What is the recessive allele frequency q?
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: light: Apply Hardy-Weinberg, testcross, mapping, and biometry
items.prompt: An organism with an unknown dominant phenotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive individual to reveal the unknown gametes. What is this cross?
options: A Hardy–Weinberg sample
An F1 intercross
A testcross
A recombination-free clone
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

Assume the model fits because the frequencies are written as symbols

items.title: entry: Explain nonselective gene-pool change
items.prompt: A flood randomly leaves a small set of survivors, and an allele becomes rare even though it did not affect survival. Which process is most direct?
options: Natural selection through differential survival
Outbreeding through mating between populations
Genetic drift through random sampling
Migration through movement of allele carriers
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: guided: Explain nonselective gene-pool change
items.prompt: A population falls from thousands to twenty after a disaster and later returns to thousands, but several alleles remain absent. What explains the persistent loss?
options: Population recovery recreated every lost allele automatically
Inbreeding converted every missing allele into a dominant allele
Outbreeding occurred despite no outside individuals entering
A bottleneck reduced the genetic diversity carried by survivors
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: light: Explain nonselective gene-pool change
items.prompt: Individuals from a neighboring population enter and reproduce, introducing an allele not previously present. Which mechanism changed the gene pool?
options: Gene flow through migration
Genetic drift without movement between populations
Inbreeding among close relatives within the original population
A bottleneck caused by random survivor sampling
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: solo: Explain nonselective gene-pool change
items.prompt: Which immediate genotype pattern is most expected when mating among relatives increases while allele frequencies initially remain fixed?
options: Fewer homozygotes and more heterozygotes
More homozygotes and fewer heterozygotes
An entirely new allele at every locus
No change in genotype proportions under any condition
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: near: Explain nonselective gene-pool change
items.prompt: A small island population shows unpredictable allele-frequency swings across generations with no trait-related reproductive difference. Which explanation fits?
options: Natural selection
Directed adaptation
Genetic drift
Obligate outbreeding
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: changed: Explain nonselective gene-pool change
items.prompt: Migrants enter a highly inbred population and mate broadly. What combined change is most likely first?
options: No allele change and increased homozygosity from outbreeding
Loss of every migrant allele before reproduction occurs
Automatic selection for the rarest allele in both populations
New allele representation and increased heterozygosity
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.prompt: Which question best separates genetic drift from natural selection?

Did the population change in any way over time?
Was the changing allele dominant rather than recessive?
Did the organisms need the allele to become more common?

Drift from a small founding sample
Inbreeding that created all founder alleles
Migration that equalized the source and new populations

Only the frequency of one phenotype without genotypes

items.title: entry: Explain natural selection, fitness, and speciation
items.prompt: Two heritable forms survive equally, but one produces twice as many fertile offspring. Which form has higher fitness in that environment?
options: The form producing more fertile offspring
The form with the longest individual lifespan
The form that appears physically larger
Both forms because their survival is equal
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: guided: Explain natural selection, fitness, and speciation
items.prompt: A heritable beak form allows more offspring to be raised during years dominated by hard seeds. What change is predicted if that environment persists?
options: Every individual changes its beak during its lifetime
Alleles associated with that beak form tend to increase
The beak form disappears because useful traits are costly
Allele frequencies remain fixed despite differential reproduction
items.directions: Select one option and commit the choice before feedback is released.

items.title: light: Explain natural selection, fitness, and speciation
items.prompt: Which observation best supports calling a population trait an adaptation?
options: One organism acquired the trait through exercise
The trait looks complex to a human observer
The heritable trait raised reproductive success in context
The population needed the trait before it appeared

items.title: solo: Explain natural selection, fitness, and speciation
items.prompt: Two alleles persist because each has higher fitness in a different recurring environment. Which outcome is most plausible?
options: Immediate fixation of both alleles at 100%
No evolutionary change because selection is absent
Automatic speciation after one generation
A maintained polymorphism

items.title: near: Explain natural selection, fitness, and speciation
items.prompt: A heritable trait raises average fertile offspring from two to five, with all else similar. What is the most direct population prediction?

The trait disappears because fitter forms reproduce less
Every organism acquires the trait before reproducing
Allele frequency changes randomly with no relation to the trait

items.title: changed: Explain natural selection, fitness, and speciation

A group benefit alone proves selection even without any reproductive difference
